claim: Many countries relied on nation-wide implementation of non-pharmaceutical intervention measures to curb the initial spread of SARS-CoV-2, resulting in substantial socio-economic impacts.
source: To curb the initial spread of SARS-CoV-2, many countries relied on nation-wide implementation of non-pharmaceutical intervention measures, resulting in substantial socio-economic impacts.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies documenting intervention measures across countries.

claim: Control of the first COVID-19 pandemic wave in the Netherlands was largely based on nation-wide implementation of a variety of non-pharmaceutical intervention measures.
source: As in many countries around the world (Brauner et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021), control of the first COVID-19 pandemic wave in the Netherlands was largely based on nation-wide implementation of a variety of non-pharmaceutical intervention measures (e.g. lockdown, social distancing, or reduced mobility).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on intervention measures and established knowledge about Dutch COVID-19 policy.

claim: The societal burden of interventions affected all areas in the Netherlands equally, while infections and healthcare burden were distributed heterogeneously across space and time.
source: Their associated societal burden affected all areas in the country equally, while infections and the healthcare burden, in contrast, were distributed heterogeneously across space and time.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of national interventions versus localized disease spread.

claim: Tailored subnational intervention strategies could prevent unnecessary broader societal burden in largely unaffected parts of a country.
source: In addition to preventing the unnecessary broader societal burden of interventions in (largely unaffected) parts of a country, such tailored strategies potentially have several additional advantages
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential benefits of subnational strategies.

claim: Subnational intervention strategies could enable more efficient use of resources, such as test kits and mobile laboratories.
source: (1) more efficient use of resources, such as test kits and mobile laboratories
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential advantages of subnational approaches.

claim: Subnational intervention strategies could reduce economic losses due to interventions.
source: (2) reduced economic losses due to interventions
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential economic benefits.

claim: Subnational intervention strategies could reduce intervention-adherence fatigue in the population.
source: (3) reducing intervention-adherence fatigue in the population.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential behavioral benefits.

claim: Epidemiological dynamics cannot easily be untangled from human behavior, which varies strongly across societies and cultures.
source: However, the challenge therein lies in the fact that epidemiological dynamics cannot easily be untangled from human behavior, which varies strongly across societies and cultures (Walker et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Walker et al., 2020.

claim: Human behavior is highly heterogeneous even within a population living in a certain geographic region.
source: and are highly heterogeneous even within a population living in a certain geographic region (Marks et al., 2021; Davies et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marks et al., 2021 and Davies et al., 2020.

claim: Epidemiological analysis needs to capture spatio-temporal heterogeneities in both transmission and control of an infectious disease.
source: For this reason, such an epidemiological analysis not only needs to capture the spatio-temporal heterogeneities in both transmission and control of an infectious disease
evidence: This is an inference based on the complexity of epidemiological dynamics.

claim: Epidemiological analysis needs to embed itself locally by considering demographic composition and how people travel, interact and mingle across different demographic groups and subnational regions.
source: but also 'to embed itself locally' (Vos et al., 2020; Eggo et al., 2021): the demographic composition of the population and how people travel, interact and mingle, across different demographic groups and subnational regions (Lloyd-Smith et al., 2005; Prem et al., 2017; Mossong et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on local embedding and demographic mixing.

claim: Intervention measures deployed in spring 2020 were not enough to spatially contain the virus.
source: By and large, intervention measures deployed in spring 2020 were not enough to spatially contain the virus
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the global spread of COVID-19.

claim: The worldwide spread of SARS-CoV-2 along the backbones of globalized travel was too fast to allow continuation of travel as usual.
source: the worldwide spread of SARS-CoV-2 along the backbones of globalized travel was too fast to allow continuation of travel as usual.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about early COVID-19 spread patterns.

claim: Reliable data on community-transmission were not readily available to researchers and policy makers during most part of the first wave.
source: Reliable data (specifically, near-real time data needed for policy-informing epidemiology) on community-transmission were not readily available to researchers and policy makers during most part of the first wave.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about data availability during early COVID-19.

claim: Large parts of the world used epidemiological insights emerging from China for setting intervention policies.
source: For setting intervention policies in such a situation, large parts of the world used epidemiological insights that were emerging from other countries that experienced the epidemic earlier, notably China (Li et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2020 and Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: National policies in the Netherlands were mostly informed by models considering populations that were demographically but not spatio-temporally heterogeneous.
source: by the time reliable data started to become available, national policies in many countries, for example, the Netherlands (RIVM, 2021a) or the UK (Kucharski et al., 2020), were mostly informed by models considering populations that were demographically but not spatio-temporally heterogeneous (Press and Levin, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to RIVM, 2021a, Kucharski et al., 2020, and Press and Levin, 2020.

claim: The first COVID-19 wave in the Netherlands covers the period February 27, 2020 to June 1, 2020.
source: The wave covers the period February 27, 2020 (the first tested case of COVID-19 in the Netherlands) till June 1, 2020 (lifting of most intervention measures).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the timeline of COVID-19 in the Netherlands.

claim: The outbreak in the Netherlands started mainly in the south of the country in relation to the celebration of Carnaval.
source: In relation to the celebration of Carnaval, an annual festivity preceding Lent that is heavily celebrated in the south of the country and is associated with large group gatherings and movement of people, the outbreak started mainly in the south of the Netherlands.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the early COVID-19 outbreak in the Netherlands.

claim: Phase 1 (Feb 27 - Mar 11) involved transmission of the pathogen progressing unchecked.
source: (i) Phase 1 (Feb 27 - Mar 11) when transmission of the pathogen progressed unchecked
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the early phase of COVID-19 in the Netherlands.

claim: Phase 2 (Mar 12 - Mar 22) involved minor interventions including working-from-home policy, cancellation of large events, some social distancing and face mask advice in specific buildings such as hospitals.
source: (ii) Phase 2 (Mar 12 - Mar 22) with minor interventions involving a working-from-home policy, cancellation of large events, some social distancing and face mask advice in specific buildings such as hospitals
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Dutch COVID-19 policy timeline.

claim: Phase 3 (Mar 23 - May 11) involved a strict nation-wide lockdown with closed schools and event centers, mandated social distancing and working-from-home policies.
source: (iii) Phase 3 (Mar 23 - May 11) involving a strict nation-wide lockdown with closed schools and event centers, mandated social distancing and working-from-home policies
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Dutch COVID-19 policy timeline.

claim: Phase 4 (May 11 - May 31) involved a gradual lifting of all measures.
source: (iv) Phase 4 (May 11 - May 31) involving a gradual lifting of all measures.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Dutch COVID-19 policy timeline.

claim: The analysis framework uses an agent-based approach with demography, mobility and mixing considerations.
source: Taking an agent-based approach, we build our framework in two parts: (i) demography, mobility and mixing considerations that provide a high-degree of local embedding
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The Dutch population was stratified into 11 demographic categories and 380 municipalities using registry data from CBS.
source: In the first step, using registry data available at the Dutch national statistics agency (CBS, Statistics Netherlands), we stratify the Dutch population into 11 demographic categories and 380 municipalities.
evidence: This describes the data source and methodology used in the study.

claim: An agent represents approximately 100 Dutch residents.
source: With about 17 million Dutch residents, we define an agent to represent approximately 100 Dutch residents.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach used in the study.

claim: Agent movements between municipalities were constructed using Dirichlet distributions based on anonymized mobile phone signals.
source: The second step is to define the probability that an agent moves between municipalities. This process is constructed using Dirichlet distributions for the probability of an agent's location, quantified based on anonymized mobile phone signals.
evidence: This describes the methodology and data source used in the study.

claim: Agent locations and movements were drawn at hourly time resolution.
source: In the third step, we draw the agent's locations and movements at hourly time resolution.
evidence: This describes the temporal resolution of the modeling approach.

claim: Mixing of agents depends on demographic category, time of day, and type of activity (home, school, work, and other).
source: The fourth step is to define the mixing of agents present within the same municipality, which depends on the demographic category of the agent, time of day and the type of activity that the agent is engaged in: 'home', 'school', 'work', and 'other'.
evidence: This describes the mixing model used in the study.

claim: Mixing matrices were based on existing surveys.
source: The corresponding mixing matrices were based on existing surveys (Prem et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Prem et al., 2017.

claim: The framework establishes a dynamic proxy network of people's contacts throughout the entire country at municipality-level with hourly resolution.
source: Together, the four steps establish a dynamic proxy network of people's contacts throughout the entire country at municipality-level, with hourly resolution over the full period of analysis.
evidence: This describes the output of the modeling framework.

claim: Initialization of the epidemic transmission model was based on observed hospital admissions, which initially occurred mainly in the south of the country.
source: Here, the fifth step concerns the initialization of the epidemic transmission model, which was based on observed hospital admissions, which initially occurred mainly in the south of the country.
evidence: This describes the data source used for model initialization.

claim: Mobility changes were computed using Google Mobility data.
source: Mobility changes were computed using Google Mobility data
evidence: This describes the data source used for quantifying mobility changes.

claim: Mixing changes were based on survey data conducted during the first wave period.
source: and mixing changes were based on survey data (Backer et al., 2021) conducted during this period.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Backer et al., 2021.

claim: The effect of behavioral measures were calibrated to reproduce the epidemic trend over time.
source: The effect of behavioral measures were calibrated to reproduce the epidemic trend over time.
evidence: This describes the calibration approach used in the study.

claim: Predicted trends in infection numbers were translated to incident and prevalent hospital admission using a simple cohort model.
source: Predicted trends in infection numbers were translated to incident and prevalent hospital admission using a simple cohort model (de Vlas and Coffeng, 2021) that accounts for the delay between initial infection and admission as well as the duration of admission.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to de Vlas and Coffeng, 2021.

claim: The cohort model was quantified based on hospitalization data from the Dutch National Intensive Care Evaluation (NICE) registration.
source: This cohort model was quantified based on hospitalization data from the Dutch National Intensive Care Evaluation (NICE) registration.
evidence: This describes the data source used for the cohort model.

claim: The calibration process was carried out by means of an ensemble of 40 stochastic simulations.
source: The results of the calibration process, carried out by means of an ensemble of 40 stochastic simulations, is shown Figure 2(a–b).
evidence: This describes the methodology used for calibration.

claim: The calibration reproduced the total national hospital admissions data spanning approximately three months.
source: to reproduce the total national hospital admissions data spanning approximately three months [panel (a)], including the (initial) doubling time [panel (b)].
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2(a-b).

claim: Hospital admissions were the most reliable source of data during the first wave.
source: Hospital admissions were the most reliable source of data during the first wave
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about data availability during early COVID-19.

claim: The model predicts that non-studying adolescents, middle-age working people, and students were the most affected demographic groups during the first wave.
source: Age stratification in our analysis reveals how the first wave likely played out nationally across demographic groups, with non-studying adolescents, middle-age working people, and students as the most affected demographic groups [Figure 2(c)].
evidence: This is based on model predictions shown in Figure 2(c).

claim: The model predicts similar patterns for seroprevalence levels across age as was observed in June 2020.
source: The model predicts similar patterns for seroprevalence levels across age as was observed in June 2020 [Appendix 2—figure 1].
evidence: This is based on comparison between model predictions and observed data.

claim: The model predicts that the epidemic geographically spread from the south to the north of the country via major cities in the west.
source: It also predicts that the epidemic geographically spread from the south (where COVID-19 is introduced in the analysis) to the north of the country via major cities in the west [Figure 2(d)].
evidence: This is based on model predictions shown in Figure 2(d).

claim: The geographic pattern of spread approximately reflects the actual spread in the Netherlands.
source: This geographic pattern approximately reflects the actual spread in the Netherlands, although we should not expect the analysis to perfectly reproduce given the high variability in the ensemble runs (see Appendix 2.4).
evidence: This is based on comparison between model predictions and observed patterns.

claim: Reductions in mobility contributed most to epidemic control during the first wave.
source: Figure 3(a), again a 40-member strong ensemble, shows how reductions in mobility contributed most to epidemic control; without mobility restrictions (red), case numbers would have approximately doubled.
evidence: This is based on model simulations shown in Figure 3(a).

claim: Without mobility restrictions, case numbers would have approximately doubled.
source: without mobility restrictions (red), case numbers would have approximately doubled.
evidence: This is based on model simulations shown in Figure 3(a).

claim: Behavioral changes had a considerable impact on epidemic control, albeit lower than mobility.
source: Behavioral changes (blue) have also had a considerable impact, albeit lower than mobility.
evidence: This is based on model simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: School closure had little impact on epidemic control during the first wave.
source: Our analysis also predicts school closure [yellow, Figure 3(a)] to have had little impact.
evidence: This is based on model simulations shown in Figure 3(a).

claim: Dutch schools were closed relatively late (March 16) due to political debate.
source: On this, we note that due to political debate, the Dutch schools were closed relatively late (March 16, while the first confirmed case was on Feb 27)
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Dutch COVID-19 policy timeline.

claim: Earlier closure of schools should have had a positive epidemiological impact.
source: (logically, earlier closure of schools should have had a positive epidemiological impact, see Appendix 2.3).
evidence: This is based on inference from model simulations shown in Appendix 2.3.

claim: Subnational interventions were implemented following the national trend by initiating lockdown when simulated prevalence of infectious cases within a municipality passed a certain threshold.
source: This means that we initiate lockdown in a municipality when the simulated prevalence of infectious cases within that municipality has passed a certain threshold — a fraction of the municipality's population — where the exact intervention measures are synchronous those issued in reality on a national scale (Appendix 1.9).
evidence: This describes the methodology for simulating subnational interventions.

claim: A lower threshold for subnational interventions ensures early implementation but could unnecessarily shut down economic and social activity in less affected areas.
source: a lower threshold ensures implementation of local interventions in an early stage of the COVID-19 wave which would suppress hospital admission counts, but could unnecessarily shut down economic and social activity in some parts of the country that are less affected by the disease.
evidence: This is an inference about the trade-offs of different threshold choices.

claim: A higher threshold for subnational interventions would target municipalities where the epidemic has progressed most but could pose the risk of starting control too late.
source: Vice versa, a higher threshold would target municipalities where the epidemic has progressed most, but could pose the risk of starting control too late, resulting in more hospital admissions.
evidence: This is an inference about the trade-offs of different threshold choices.

claim: Thresholds of 3%, 1%, 0.33%, and 0.1% prevalence of infectious cases were tested for subnational interventions.
source: To show the effect of different thresholds for prevalence of infectious cases, we choose a wide range of 3%, 1%, 0.33%, and 0.1%.
evidence: This describes the scenarios tested in the study.

claim: The national lockdown as implemented in the Netherlands resulted in approximately 13 thousand hospital admissions up to 1 June 2020.
source: In panel (a), the lockdown as implemented in the Netherlands is represented by the black (observed) and green lines (prediction), which resulted in approximately 13 thousand hospital admissions up to 1 June 2020.
evidence: This is based on observed data and model predictions shown in Figure 4(a).

claim: A threshold of 3% for subnational interventions provided 185 million additional person-days intervention-free over the full wave.
source: (185 million additional person-days intervention-free over the full wave)
evidence: This is based on model simulations.

claim: Thresholds of 1.0% and 0.33% for subnational interventions resulted in 4670 and 410 additional hospital admissions, respectively, compared to the national lockdown.
source: The more stringent thresholds of 1.0% and 0.33% result in numbers of hospital admissions closer to a national lockdown (4670 and 410 additional admissions, respectively)
evidence: This is based on model simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: Thresholds of 1.0% and 0.33% for subnational interventions resulted in 268 and 167 municipalities initializing interventions later than in the national approach, respectively.
source: but at a more modest societal benefit: 268 and 167 municipalities initialize interventions later than in the national approach, respectively.
evidence: This is based on model simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: Thresholds of 1.0% and 0.33% for subnational interventions provided 103 million and 36 million additional person-days free from interventions, respectively.
source: This translates to 103 million and 36 million additional person-days free from interventions over the full period.
evidence: This is based on model simulations.

claim: At the 0.33% threshold, approximately 6% of municipalities never undergo interventions.
source: Interestingly, at the lower threshold of 0.33% (orange), approximately 6% of the municipalities never undergo interventions.
evidence: This is based on model simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: A threshold of 0.1% for subnational interventions yields only a few additional hospital admissions with 18 municipalities remaining intervention-free for over 5 weeks.
source: Even closer to the fully national approach, we also tested a threshold of 0.1% (yellow), which yields only a few additional hospital admissions, and still 18 municipalities remaining intervention-free for over 5 weeks.
evidence: This is based on model simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: Municipalities that remain free of interventions are mainly located in the north and east of the country.
source: Municipalities that remain free of interventions are mainly located in the north and east of the country, as can be most clearly seen for the 0.33% threshold scenario.
evidence: This is based on model simulations shown in Figure 4(d).

claim: From a mobility perspective, municipalities remaining free of interventions belong to the more rural, isolated, and less densely populated subnational regions.
source: From a mobility perspective, these municipalities belong to the more rural, isolated, and less densely populated subnational regions of the country.
evidence: This is an inference based on the geographic distribution of municipalities and mobility patterns.

claim: During the first COVID-19 wave, the Dutch government did not implement subnational intervention measures aside from an early advice to work from home in the south.
source: During the first COVID-19 wave, the Dutch government did not implement subnational intervention measures, aside from bringing out an early advice to work from home in the south of the country, the epicenter for the first wave.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Dutch COVID-19 policy.

claim: The Dutch government's reasoning for not implementing subnational measures was that once COVID-19 cases were discovered locally, the pathogen would have likely already spread throughout the entire country.
source: The reasoning was that once COVID-19 cases were discovered locally, most likely, the pathogen would have already spread throughout the entire country.
evidence: This describes the rationale behind Dutch policy decisions.

claim: The Netherlands is spatially well-connected in terms of people's mobility patterns, facilitated by a robust public transport system and a high population density.
source: This is generally in line with observations that the Netherlands is spatially well-connected in terms of people's mobility patterns, facilitated by a robust public transport system and a high population density
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Dutch infrastructure and demographics.

claim: Hospital admission data during the first wave suggested that provinces in the north and east of the Netherlands were substantially less affected.
source: with the caveat that hospital admission data during the first wave did suggest that provinces in the north and east of the country were substantially less affected.
evidence: This is based on observed hospital admission data.

claim: When combined with live tracking of local infections, implementation of interventions could be postponed or tailored towards local contexts without causing too much additional health burden.
source: Our results show that when combined with live tracking of local infections in sufficient detail, implementation of interventions could be postponed or tailored towards local contexts, without causing too much additional health burden.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model results.

claim: Subnational implementation of interventions would require local governments to be mandated appropriately and local populations to adhere to local measures.
source: (This would of course require local governments to be mandated appropriately and that local populations adhere to local measures.)
evidence: This is a speculative statement about requirements for implementing subnational interventions.

claim: The framework does not provide insights into the role of households and household-level interventions.
source: As such, our framework cannot provide insights into the role of households and household-level interventions, which have for instance been shown to play a critical role in the geographical spread of infection between schools (Munday et al., 2021; Lessler et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors, with citations to relevant studies.

claim: Mobile phone signal data do not provide identifiers to link multiple movements into one itinerary.
source: As such, the data do not provide identifiers to link multiple movements into one itinerary, which means that in our analysis, agent movements are somewhat shorter on average than in reality, but agents also visit more different locations than in reality.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the data source used.

claim: The impact of the simplifying assumption about agent movements is limited at the start of an epidemic, especially in a relatively small and highly connected country.
source: However, the impact of this simplifying assumption is limited as, at the start of an epidemic, the distribution of movement over agents is of relatively low importance, especially in the case of a relatively small and highly connected country as the Netherlands.
evidence: This is an inference about the impact of modeling assumptions.

claim: The transmission potential of 'high-mobility corridors' can eventually dry up as a result of rising immunity among high-mobility individuals in larger geographies.
source: This is in contrast to situations towards the tail of an epidemic or in larger geographies (e.g. Brazil [Castro et al., 2021; de Souza et al., 2020] and India [Laxminarayan et al., 2020]), where the transmission potential of 'high-mobility corridors' can eventually dry up as a result of rising immunity among high-mobility individuals.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in Brazil and India.

claim: The study adopted data on national patterns in mobility, meaning it was not possible to account for changes in mobility by geography or demographic group.
source: Finally, we adopted data on national patterns in mobility (Google mobility), meaning that it was not possible to account for changes in mobility by geography or demographic group.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the data source used.

claim: Geographical aspects of mobility could be addressed by using longitudinal mobile phone signal data or individual-level self-reported data via mobile phone apps.
source: The geographical aspects could be addressed by using longitudinal mobile phone signal data or individual-level self-reported data via mobile phone apps (Drew et al., 2020; Oliver et al., 2020; Ferretti et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future work, supported by citations.

claim: With appropriate data sources, the framework can be adapted to other countries and settings of similar or larger geographical scale.
source: With appropriate data sources, the framework can be adapted to other countries and settings of similar or larger geographical scale.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the generalizability of the framework.

claim: Specifically isolating affected subnational areas could reduce hospital admissions by about 30% compared to the actual national lockdown.
source: For instance, we explored the potential impact of specifically isolating affected subnational areas (i.e. banning all mobility into and out of a municipality for the Netherlands), which could reduce hospital admissions by about 30%, compared to the actual national lockdown (Appendix 2.3).
evidence: This is based on model simulations shown in Appendix 2.3.

claim: With further expansions, the framework could address questions related to closing or limiting specific transport routes.
source: With further expansions, the framework could address questions related to, for instance, closing or limiting specific (public) transport routes (Quilty et al., 2020)
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications, with citation.

claim: The framework could address questions related to banning specific mass events.
source: and banning specific mass events (Herng et al., 2022; Moritz et al., 2021; Lemieux et al., 2021)
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications, with citations.

claim: Evaluating pharmaceutical interventions such as vaccination is possible within this framework upon coupling data sources associated with age-stratified vaccination rollout and types of vaccines used.
source: Evaluating pharmaceutical interventions such as vaccination, too, is possible to capture within this framework, upon coupling data sources associated with age-stratified vaccination rollout, as well as types of vaccines used.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications.

claim: For the Dutch case, 167 municipalities could have remained open at the start with only 3.4% more hospital admissions, with 12 still open after five weeks.
source: For the Dutch case, we calculate explicitly how many municipalities could have remained open with limited additional hospital admissions: 167 at the start and 12 still open after five weeks, with only 3.4% more hospital admissions.
evidence: This is based on model simulations.

claim: The Netherlands has a high population density and is highly interlinked in terms of mobility, but even there a subnational approach would have benefited the intervention strategy.
source: The Netherlands has a high population density and is highly interlinked in terms of mobility, but even there a subnational approach would have benefited the intervention strategy — which does create high expectations of similar approaches in other countries.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model results and characteristics of the Netherlands.

claim: The results create high expectations that similar subnational approaches would benefit other countries.
source: which does create high expectations of similar approaches in other countries.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the study results.

claim: The main merit of the approach lies in capturing the local context by coupling empirical data sources on demography, mobility, and spatial clustering of the population and linking this to disease transmission.
source: Third, in terms of methodology, the main merit of our approach lies in the fact that it captures the local context by coupling empirical data sources on demography, mobility, and spatial clustering of the population and link this to disease transmission.
evidence: This describes the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: The approach makes it possible to decouple individual interventions such as mobility reduction and behavioral changes.
source: Additionally, we show how to decouple individual interventions in Figure 3, which is made possible by capturing the local context: mobility reduction and behavioral changes cannot be separated if mobility and behavior are not explicitly modeled.
evidence: This describes a methodological capability demonstrated in the study.

claim: Whether subnational implementation of interventions is sufficient to successfully control an epidemic should be expected to vary across countries and cultures.
source: That said, whether subnational implementation of interventions is sufficient to successfully control an epidemic should be expected to vary across countries and cultures, as its effectiveness depends on its timeliness and feasibility, and it being sufficiently supported and/or enforceable.
evidence: This is an inference about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: Subnational control measures worked in China due to high enforcement and feasibility.
source: For example, subnational control measures worked (to some extent) in China due to high enforcement and feasibility (sheer man power)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sachs et al., 2022.

claim: Subnational control measures worked in New Zealand and Australia due to natural long distances between subpopulations and relative isolation from the rest of the globe.
source: and in New Zealand and Australia due natural long distances between subpopulations and relative isolation from the rest of the globe (Sachs et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sachs et al., 2022.

claim: During the initial wave in Northern Italy, the regional lockdown was implemented too late to curb further geographical spread.
source: In contrast, during the initial wave in Northern Italy which is a highly connected region, the regional lockdown was implemented too late to curb further geographical spread (Waitzberg et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Waitzberg et al., 2022.

claim: Demographic data provided by Statistics Netherlands allowed distinguishing 170,721 agents with demographic details.
source: Additionally, the demographic data provided by Statistics Netherlands (CBS) allowed us to distinguish 170,721 agents (with roughly 17 million residents, this means that each agent represents about 100 of them) with demographic details (Appendix 1.1).
evidence: This describes the data source and agent representation used in the study.

claim: Generated mobility distributions are Dirichlet distributions using normalized movements data as shape parameters.
source: More specifically, the generated mobility distributions are Dirichlet distributions, using the (normalized) movements data as shape parameters.
evidence: This describes the statistical method used for mobility modeling.

claim: The first COVID-19 wave in the Netherlands lasted from February 27 to June 1, 2020.
source: The first COVID-19 wave in the Netherlands lasted over the period February 27 (first reported case) to June 1, 2020.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the timeline of COVID-19 in the Netherlands.

claim: Phase 2 involved a 31.7% reduction in travel.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: Phase 3 involved a 42.4% reduction in travel.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: Phase 4 involved a 20.1% reduction in travel.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: The dominant contribution to travel reduction was due to a working-from-home policy recommended by the Dutch government.
source: The dominant contribution to this travel reduction, by far, was due to a working-from-home policy recommended by the Dutch government
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Dutch COVID-19 policy.

claim: Changes in mixing patterns were determined from Dutch survey data in February, April, and June 2020.
source: Secondly, we address changes in mixing patterns by determining percentage changes in the mixing among different age groups from Dutch survey data (Backer et al., 2021) in the months February, April, and June 2020
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Backer et al., 2021.

claim: School closing was implemented by placing school-going agents and parents of primary school children at home in terms of location and mixing implications.
source: Fourth and finally, we implement school closing by placing school-going agents (i.e. primary school children, secondary school children and students) as well as the parents of primary school children at home, both in terms of the home locations of the agents and in terms of its implications on mixing (see Appendix 1.5).
evidence: This describes the methodology for implementing school closure in the model.
